title: Corporate Strategy Vertical Integration and Diversification

questions.stem: A board member argues: 'Licensing is effectively ownership.' The most accurate correction is:

options.A: Licensing removes opportunism entirely, while ownership increases opportunism in practice.
options.B: Ownership is identical to licensing, since both transfer control to the buyer.
options.C: Contracts can reduce hazards, but ownership changes residual control rights and incentives.
options.D: Contracts fully replicate ownership, so governance choice is always irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Ownership reallocates residual control rights and authority; contracts can never fully specify all contingencies at reasonable cost.

questions.stem: A selective hybrid where Apple makes modems for some SKUs but buys for others is closest to:

options.A: A pure outsourcing choice because any external sourcing dominates governance form.
options.B: A hybrid governance arrangement that mixes make and buy to preserve benchmarking.
options.C: An unrelated diversification choice because the supplier market is separate.
options.D: A full integration choice because any internal production ends external dependence.

questions.explanation: Hybrid governance sits between market and hierarchy: it can support learning and benchmarking while limiting commitment and rigidity.

questions.stem: A subtle risk of internalising modems even if per-unit cost falls is:

options.A: Automatic economies of scope because modems create synergy across unrelated units.
options.B: Guaranteed legal immunity because internal ownership reduces compliance exposure.
options.C: Reduced flexibility when technology standards shift faster than internal capability can adapt.
options.D: Elimination of coordination cost because ownership removes complexity entirely.

questions.explanation: Vertical integration can increase rigidity and fixed-cost commitment; the firm may be slower to pivot if standards and performance requirements change.

questions.stem: Acquiring a specialist modem team (tuck-in) is best interpreted as:

options.A: A business-level positioning move that does not change firm boundaries.
options.B: A horizontal diversification into unrelated industries with no device linkage at all.
options.C: A geographic expansion into new markets because talent is distributed globally.
options.D: An instrument to move toward make by buying capability and partial control rights.

questions.explanation: Tuck-ins are a mechanism of boundary change: they can accelerate internal capability and shift the firm toward 'make' without changing customer markets.

questions.stem: Apple internalising a modem subsystem is vertical integration rather than horizontal diversification because:

options.A: It expands countries served, so it is geographic scope in most cases.
options.B: It changes who performs a value-chain activity, not which customer markets are served.
options.C: It changes pricing strategy, so it is business strategy by default.
options.D: It adds a new revenue stream, so it is diversification by definition.

questions.explanation: Vertical integration concerns ownership/inside-outside decisions for activities in the value chain, not entry into new customer markets.

questions.stem: Apple shifting from licensed Qualcomm modems to an in-house modem mainly changes which corporate strategy dimension?

options.A: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated product markets beyond device ecosystems.
options.B: Vertical scope by internalising an upstream activity previously purchased externally.
options.C: Business-level strategy by selecting cost leadership over differentiation in practice.
options.D: Geographic scope by widening the countries where devices are sold and supported.

questions.explanation: Internalising a component stage moves an activity from market to firm, changing vertical boundaries (vertical integration scope). It is not a geographic or horizontal diversification move.

questions.stem: Continuing to rely on Qualcomm under licensing is best classified on the make-or-buy continuum as:

options.A: A parent-subsidiary relation because licensing implies ownership and integration.
options.B: A make choice because licensing implies internal production and ownership control.
options.C: A buy choice using contracts/licensing with residual control rights staying external.
options.D: A joint venture because both parties share governance and operating decisions.

questions.explanation: Licensing/purchasing is 'buy' governance: the activity remains outside firm boundaries and residual control rights stay with the supplier.

questions.stem: If Apple buys an unrelated insurance business with no competence transfer, that is:

options.A: Unrelated diversification beyond a single market without synergy basis.
options.B: A geographic scope move because insurance is regulated nationally.
options.C: Backward vertical integration into upstream component production and supply.
options.D: Forward vertical integration into downstream distribution of device products.

questions.explanation: This changes horizontal scope into an unrelated industry; absent competence transfer, it is unrelated diversification.

questions.stem: If Apple expects rapid modem standard shifts, the most defensible first move is often:

options.A: Immediate geographic expansion because standards vary by country always.
options.B: Immediate full integration because volatility makes contracts unenforceable.
options.C: Hybrid governance that preserves flexibility while building internal capability gradually.
options.D: Immediate unrelated diversification to hedge the risk through portfolio logic.

questions.explanation: Under uncertainty, hybrids can preserve flexibility and allow learning; full integration can lock the firm into fixed costs and rigid commitments.

questions.stem: If Apple internalises modems mainly to weaken supplier bargaining power, the motive is closest to:

options.A: Building economies of scope by sharing capabilities across unrelated businesses.
options.B: Expanding geographic scope by entering new countries with different regulation.
options.C: Increasing market power by reducing dependence on an external bottleneck partner.
options.D: Reducing risk by diversifying across unrelated industries and financial assets.

questions.explanation: A growth motive in Chapter 8 is market power: reducing dependence on a powerful supplier can increase bargaining leverage, though it may raise internal costs.

questions.stem: If Apple internalises to reduce renegotiation hazard and dependence, the best theoretical justification is:

options.A: Platform logic under cross-side network effects and multi-homing behavior.
options.B: Blue-ocean logic under value innovation and new-demand creation dynamics.
options.C: Industry life-cycle logic under introduction and shakeout stage pressures.
options.D: Transaction-cost logic under contracting hazards and asset specificity concerns.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 uses transaction-cost reasoning: when markets are risky due to hazards (e.g., opportunism, enforceability), internalisation can reduce total governance cost.

questions.stem: If Apple makes modems for one product line mainly to learn while buying for iPhones, the cleanest label is:

options.A: A full backward integration move that eliminates reliance on external suppliers fully.
options.B: A staged hybrid that uses internal production for learning and external sourcing for benchmarking.
options.C: A geographic scope shift because product lines are sold in different regions.
options.D: A related diversification move because product lines are different industries in effect.

questions.explanation: Selective internalisation is a learning-and-benchmarking hybrid on the make-or-buy continuum; it is not full integration.

questions.stem: If Apple uses long-horizon contracts plus partial internal production, the best label is:

options.A: A pure buy choice because any contract implies external governance only.
options.B: A portfolio of governance forms chosen to minimise total transaction and coordination costs.
options.C: A geographic scope choice because contracts differ across regions in practice.
options.D: A pure make choice because internal production exists at least somewhere.

questions.explanation: Firms can mix governance forms by activity, product line, or region; the goal is to reduce total governance costs while preserving capability and flexibility.

questions.stem: The most disciplined Chapter 8 test for the modem decision is whether:

options.A: Short-run margin rises, because corporate strategy is always a quarterly choice.
options.B: Total value created exceeds governance, coordination, and capability-build costs.
options.C: Competitor imitation occurs quickly, because imitation signals strategic correctness.
options.D: Media sentiment improves, because corporate scope is primarily reputational capital.

questions.explanation: Corporate strategy is judged by net value creation: benefits (cost, quality, risk) must exceed coordination costs, rigidity, and capability-development burdens.

questions.stem: Which action is least likely to be a corporate strategy move under Chapter 8 framing?

options.A: Optimising an internal modem-testing protocol without changing ownership boundaries.
options.B: Forming an equity alliance to share control rights over a key input.
options.C: Divesting a business unit to reduce horizontal scope and complexity.
options.D: Acquiring a supplier capability to internalise a value-chain stage.

questions.explanation: Corporate strategy concerns scope and boundaries; internal process improvement is operational effectiveness within existing boundaries.

questions.stem: Which choice is an example of a boundary alternative to full integration emphasized in Chapter 8?

options.A: Unrelated diversification into finance to hedge volatility in chip supply markets.
options.B: Long-horizon contracts or equity alliances that align incentives without full ownership.
options.C: Geographic expansion into new countries while keeping sourcing unchanged.
options.D: Spot-market bidding with frequent switching to maximize short-term flexibility.

questions.explanation: Alternatives include longer contracts, equity alliances, joint ventures, and taper/hybrid approaches that reduce hazards without full ownership.

questions.stem: Which governance form sits closest to 'make' on the continuum?

options.A: Equity alliance with partial ownership but shared control rights.
options.B: Full internal performance of the activity within the firm's boundary.
options.C: Long-term contracting with penalties and audit clauses for performance.
options.D: Spot purchasing from multiple suppliers with rapid switching ability.

questions.explanation: Full internal performance is closest to 'make' because residual control rights are inside the firm; the others remain external or hybrid.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of Chapter 8's three corporate strategy dimensions?

options.A: Geographic scope across regions and national markets.
options.B: Innovation cadence and imitation timing across technology life cycles.
options.C: Vertical integration scope along the value chain stages.
options.D: Horizontal diversification scope beyond one product-market domain.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 assesses corporate strategy along vertical scope, horizontal scope, and geographic scope. Innovation cadence is treated elsewhere in the text.

questions.stem: Which is the best 'non-intuitive' warning when executives say 'control is always good'?

options.A: Control always improves margins because internal costs are always lower.
options.B: Control can be value destroying when added coordination and rigidity exceed benefits.
options.C: Control always reduces scrutiny because regulators prefer integrated firms.
options.D: Control always eliminates risk because ownership removes uncertainty completely.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 stresses that corporate moves must create net value; control can increase cost, reduce flexibility, and raise liability.

questions.stem: Which is the most accurate description of 'vertical market failure' in Chapter 8?

options.A: Markets are global so vertical integration is legally impossible everywhere in practice at scale.
options.B: Markets create scope economies automatically so diversification is unnecessary in practice at scale.
options.C: Markets along the value chain are too risky and alternatives too costly in time or money.
options.D: Markets are perfectly competitive so the firm should always buy the activity in practice.

questions.explanation: Vertical market failure occurs when market governance is too risky or alternatives too costly, making integration or hybrids attractive.

questions.stem: Which of the following best fits a diversification premium condition?

options.A: Unrelated businesses reduce risk, so valuations always rise above sum-of-parts.
options.B: Shared capabilities create economies of scope that exceed added coordination costs.
options.C: Geographic expansion always creates synergy, so valuations rise mechanically.
options.D: Spinouts always destroy value because internal markets are weakened.

questions.explanation: A premium requires real scope economies or other value creation exceeding the costs of complexity; unrelated risk reduction alone is not guaranteed to create premiums.

questions.stem: Which option is most likely to increase legal exposure rather than reduce it?

options.A: Keeping activity external under licensing with supplier bearing some obligations.
options.B: Using a joint venture where liabilities are ring-fenced by governance terms.
options.C: Using long-horizon contracts with explicit audit rights and service levels.
options.D: Owning and operating sensitive design and compliance processes inside the firm.

questions.explanation: Internalisation can increase compliance responsibilities and legal exposure; outsourcing or structured governance can sometimes shift or share that burden.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures why 'make' can raise cost even when the supplier is expensive?

options.A: Internal units guarantee scale economies bigger than the whole industry.
options.B: Internal units eliminate fixed costs because capex disappears in practice.
options.C: Internal units can lose market discipline and create higher overhead over time.
options.D: Internal units always face more competition, which forces costs down sharply.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 notes in-house suppliers may not be exposed to competitive pressure, potentially increasing cost structures and inefficiency.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes why 'shorter option is correct' is unreliable here?

options.A: Option length is controlled, so correctness depends on concept logic not style.
options.B: Option length signals expertise, so longer options are always correct.
options.C: Option length is irrelevant because all corporate strategy is subjective.
options.D: Option length signals difficulty, so shorter options are always correct.

questions.explanation: The quiz is designed so option length does not cue correctness; students must apply the Chapter 8 logic precisely.

questions.stem: Which statement most precisely separates corporate strategy from business strategy in this case?

options.A: Corporate strategy sets marketing spend; business strategy sets diversification typology only.
options.B: Corporate strategy sets pricing tactics; business strategy sets ownership boundaries and scope.
options.C: Corporate strategy sets HR policy; business strategy sets geography and vertical scope.
options.D: Corporate strategy sets firm boundaries; business strategy sets how to compete within an arena.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 treats corporate strategy as boundary and scope decisions (vertical/horizontal/geographic). Business strategy concerns competitive positioning within a given industry.

questions.stem: A delivery joint venture is best classified as:

options.A: A geographic expansion arrangement because partners operate in multiple states.
options.B: A hybrid governance arrangement with shared control rights and joint decision making.
options.C: A parent-subsidiary arrangement with full control and no shared governance rights.
options.D: A spot-market arrangement where switching is costless and continuity is absent.

questions.explanation: Joint ventures create shared governance and allocate control rights; they are intermediate forms on the make-or-buy continuum.

questions.stem: A delivery joint venture is best classified as:

options.A: A spot-market arrangement where switching is costless and continuity is absent.
options.B: A parent-subsidiary arrangement with full control and no shared governance rights.
options.C: A hybrid governance arrangement with shared control rights and joint decision making.
options.D: A geographic expansion arrangement because partners operate in multiple states.

questions.explanation: Joint ventures create shared governance and allocate control rights; they are intermediate forms on the make-or-buy continuum.

questions.stem: A non-intuitive risk of full forward integration into last-mile delivery is:

options.A: Elimination of legal and safety compliance because internal fleets reduce scrutiny.
options.B: Higher fixed cost and reduced flexibility when demand or labor conditions shift.
options.C: Guaranteed on-time performance because internal delivery always outperforms in practice.
options.D: Automatic reduction of coordination burdens because ownership removes conflict.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 warns integration can reduce flexibility and raise fixed costs; regulatory and labor constraints may increase internal complexity.

questions.stem: Amazon expanding delivery stations and rural coverage is best classified as:

options.A: Unrelated diversification into transport manufacturing with no e-commerce linkage.
options.B: Backward vertical integration into upstream packaging materials and supplier stages.
options.C: Geographic scope expansion only because facilities are domestic and regional.
options.D: Forward vertical integration into downstream fulfilment and last-mile delivery capacity.

questions.explanation: Owning more distribution nodes and delivery capacity internalises downstream activities, which is forward vertical integration in the value chain.

questions.stem: Claim: 'This is only geography, not corporate strategy.' Best correction is:

options.A: Facilities can still change vertical scope by internalising activities previously outsourced.
options.B: It is unrelated diversification because delivery is a different industry.
options.C: Only mergers change boundaries, so facility build-out is operational only.
options.D: Domestic facilities never change boundaries because they remain in one country.

questions.explanation: A corporate boundary shift can occur within a country; internalisation changes who performs the activity.

questions.stem: If Amazon internalises last-mile mainly to reduce carrier bargaining power, the motive is:

options.A: Risk reduction by unrelated diversification across non-logistics business units.
options.B: Geographic scope expansion because bargaining differs by country regulation.
options.C: Market power by reducing dependence on a bottleneck partner and improving leverage.
options.D: Economies of scope because carriers create synergy across unrelated industries.

questions.explanation: Reducing dependence on a powerful partner can increase leverage; it is a market power motive, not diversification.

questions.stem: If Amazon uses USPS for low-density routes but its own fleet for dense routes, this is:

options.A: An unrelated diversification strategy because route types are different industries.
options.B: A full buy strategy because any USPS use implies markets dominate governance.
options.C: A full make strategy because any internal delivery ends all outsourcing.
options.D: A selective hybrid boundary strategy balancing cost economics of density.

questions.explanation: This is selective internalisation: governance differs by route economics; it is a hybrid strategy.

questions.stem: If delivery quality is observable but contract enforcement is costly, the best implication is:

options.A: Integration never helps because contracts can fully specify and enforce quality.
options.B: Governance may shift toward hybrids or internalisation to secure performance.
options.C: Geographic expansion solves enforcement by averaging quality across regions.
options.D: Markets perfectly replicate ownership because observability solves enforcement.

questions.explanation: Even observable performance can be hard to enforce due to monitoring and legal costs; governance may change accordingly.

questions.stem: In Chapter 8 terms, building new delivery stations primarily changes:

options.A: Vertical scope by internalising distribution capacity and fulfilment activities.
options.B: Geographic scope by entering new countries and new regulatory jurisdictions.
options.C: Business strategy by repositioning in rivalry without boundary changes.
options.D: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated markets with no competence overlap.

questions.explanation: This is a boundary/vertical scope decision (distribution stage ownership), not horizontal diversification.

questions.stem: In Chapter 8 terms, building new delivery stations primarily changes:

options.A: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated markets with no competence overlap.
options.B: Business strategy by repositioning in rivalry without boundary changes.
options.C: Geographic scope by entering new countries and new regulatory jurisdictions.
options.D: Vertical scope by internalising distribution capacity and fulfilment activities.

questions.explanation: This is a boundary/vertical scope decision (distribution stage ownership), not horizontal diversification.

questions.stem: In Chapter 8 terms, building new delivery stations primarily changes:

options.A: Geographic scope by entering new countries and new regulatory jurisdictions.
options.B: Vertical scope by internalising distribution capacity and fulfilment activities.
options.C: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated markets with no competence overlap.
options.D: Business strategy by repositioning in rivalry without boundary changes.

questions.explanation: This is a boundary/vertical scope decision (distribution stage ownership), not horizontal diversification.

questions.stem: Long-horizon contracts with carriers fit Chapter 8 primarily as:

options.A: A spot market buy identical to short-term switching and no continuity.
options.B: A pure make choice equivalent to internalising carrier assets and labor control.
options.C: A diversification move because contracts create a new revenue business.
options.D: A hybrid governance form that reduces hazards without full ownership integration.

questions.explanation: Long-term contracts can enable investment and reduce opportunism while keeping activities outside firm boundaries.

questions.stem: Reducing reliance on USPS by shifting volume to Amazon's own network is closest to:

options.A: A move toward business strategy because logistics never changes boundaries.
options.B: A move toward make by internalising delivery rather than buying from carriers.
options.C: A move toward geographic scope because rural routes imply national expansion.
options.D: A move toward unrelated diversification because delivery is a separate industry.

questions.explanation: This is a boundary decision: internalising a stage that was outsourced moves governance toward 'make'.

questions.stem: Taper logistics (own fleet plus carriers) is best justified when Amazon wants:

options.A: Diversification premium by adding unrelated businesses alongside logistics.
options.B: Flexibility plus benchmarking under peak-season volatility and uncertain capacity.
options.C: Elimination of all contracting costs and compliance costs by owning everything.
options.D: Guaranteed lowest price by forcing monthly auctions among many carriers.

questions.explanation: Taper integration combines internal capacity and external sourcing to preserve flexibility and allow benchmarking of cost and quality.

questions.stem: The most disciplined criterion for deeper integration is:

options.A: Short-run share price because it fully reveals long-run synergy and learning.
options.B: Competitor response because protests imply the move must create value.
options.C: Net value after including rigidity, fixed cost, coordination burden, and liability.
options.D: Management preference because corporate scope is untestable and subjective.

questions.explanation: Corporate moves must create net value; a correct evaluation includes costs of control, rigidity, and governance burdens.

questions.stem: The most disciplined criterion for deeper integration is:

options.A: Net value after including rigidity, fixed cost, coordination burden, and liability.
options.B: Management preference because corporate scope is untestable and subjective.
options.C: Competitor response because protests imply the move must create value.
options.D: Short-run share price because it fully reveals long-run synergy and learning.

questions.explanation: Corporate moves must create net value; a correct evaluation includes costs of control, rigidity, and governance burdens.

questions.stem: Which alternative is an 'alternative to integration' that still aligns incentives?

options.A: Equity alliance or joint venture with a carrier to share control rights and risk.
options.B: Unrelated diversification into unrelated industries to hedge logistics volatility in practice.
options.C: Geographic expansion to new countries without changing logistics governance in practice.
options.D: Short-term spot bidding with rapid switching to maximize pressure on suppliers.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 emphasizes alliances/JVs and long-term contracts as alternatives to full integration, especially when hazards exist but full ownership is too costly.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes forward integration from geographic expansion?

options.A: Forward integration is business strategy; geographic scope is corporate strategy.
options.B: Forward integration changes stage ownership; geographic scope changes where to compete.
options.C: Forward integration changes where to compete; geographic scope changes ownership.
options.D: Forward integration is unrelated diversification; geographic scope is vertical.

questions.explanation: Forward integration concerns ownership of downstream stages; geographic scope concerns the spatial markets where the firm competes.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes forward integration from geographic expansion?

options.A: Forward integration changes stage ownership; geographic scope changes where to compete.
options.B: Forward integration is business strategy; geographic scope is corporate strategy.
options.C: Forward integration changes where to compete; geographic scope changes ownership.
options.D: Forward integration is unrelated diversification; geographic scope is vertical.

questions.explanation: Forward integration concerns ownership of downstream stages; geographic scope concerns the spatial markets where the firm competes.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes forward integration from geographic expansion?

options.A: Forward integration changes stage ownership; geographic scope changes where to compete.
options.B: Forward integration changes where to compete; geographic scope changes ownership.
options.C: Forward integration is business strategy; geographic scope is corporate strategy.
options.D: Forward integration is unrelated diversification; geographic scope is vertical.

questions.explanation: Forward integration concerns ownership of downstream stages; geographic scope concerns the spatial markets where the firm competes.

questions.stem: Why can internal logistics raise cost even if carriers are expensive?

options.A: Internal units may lose market discipline and develop higher overhead structures.
options.B: Internal units guarantee cost curves below the industry frontier over time.
options.C: Internal units eliminate capex because ownership replaces investment entirely.
options.D: Internal units face more competition, which forces costs down quickly at scale.

questions.explanation: Vertical integration can raise costs if internal operations become inefficient or if scale is insufficient; market discipline can be weaker internally.

questions.stem: A non-intuitive risk of upstream integration emphasized in Chapter 8 is:

options.A: Automatic elimination of commodity price volatility because ownership stabilises prices.
options.B: Guaranteed quality because internal production always outperforms suppliers.
options.C: Guaranteed cost advantage because internal operations always beat spot markets.
options.D: Environmental and compliance liability that becomes owned rather than contracted out.

questions.explanation: Owning upstream stages can increase legal exposure, environmental liability, and compliance obligations; it does not automatically stabilise prices or guarantee cost advantage.

questions.stem: Backward integration makes the most sense when:

options.A: Inputs are commodities, switching is easy, and many suppliers exist globally.
options.B: Quality is fully enforceable at low cost through complete contracts.
options.C: Contracting hazards and dependence risks are high and capability fit is credible.
options.D: Demand is perfectly stable, so volatility never affects governance choice.

questions.explanation: Transaction-cost logic supports integration when markets are risky or costly due to hazards; stable commodity markets often favour buying.

questions.stem: If lithium prices fall sharply after integration, the best described integration risk is:

options.A: Fixed-cost exposure and reduced flexibility relative to buying at market prices.
options.B: Elimination of volatility because internal ownership stabilises commodity prices.
options.C: Guaranteed cost advantage because internal operations always remain cheaper.
options.D: Automatic diversification premium because investors always reward integration.

questions.explanation: Integration can lock the firm into fixed costs; when market prices drop, the firm may be stuck with higher internal cost structure than buying.

questions.stem: Ola Electric deploying in-house cells and packs is most directly a move toward:

options.A: Unrelated diversification because cell manufacturing is a separate industry always.
options.B: Geographic scope expansion because domestic plants imply new markets.
options.C: Forward integration to control retailing and downstream distribution channels.
options.D: Backward integration to secure a critical input and reduce dependence on suppliers.

questions.explanation: Cell and pack production are upstream inputs into vehicle production; owning them is backward integration under Chapter 8.

questions.stem: Taper integration for critical battery inputs would mean:

options.A: Owning some internal capacity while still buying a meaningful share externally.
options.B: Using only spot markets with no relationships to preserve flexibility always.
options.C: Outsourcing everything upstream while keeping only branding and assembly.
options.D: Owning all upstream and downstream stages and cutting all suppliers immediately.

questions.explanation: Taper integration mixes internal and external sourcing, enabling benchmarking and flexibility under volatility.

questions.stem: Tesla building an in-house lithium refinery is best classified as:

options.A: Forward vertical integration into downstream retail showrooms and service networks.
options.B: Horizontal diversification into unrelated industries with no battery linkage at all.
options.C: Geographic scope expansion only because the facility is domestic in location.
options.D: Backward vertical integration into upstream input processing and supply security.

questions.explanation: Lithium refining is upstream in the battery value chain; internalising it is backward integration to secure critical inputs.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest alternative to full integration that still aligns incentives?

options.A: Unrelated diversification into other industries to hedge supply chain volatility.
options.B: Monthly spot bidding to intensify switching and prevent any supplier lock-in.
options.C: Long-term contracts or equity alliances that support supplier investment and stability.
options.D: Geographic expansion to new markets without changing supplier governance.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 highlights long-term contracting and equity alliances/JVs as alternatives to full ownership when hazards exist but integration is costly.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest alternative to full integration that still aligns incentives?

options.B: Long-term contracts or equity alliances that support supplier investment and stability.
options.C: Geographic expansion to new markets without changing supplier governance.
options.D: Unrelated diversification into other industries to hedge supply chain volatility.

questions.explanation: Chapter 8 highlights long-term contracting and equity alliances/JVs as alternatives to full ownership when hazards exist but integration is costly.

questions.stem: Which specificity type best matches equipment engineered for one buyer's component tolerances?

options.A: Physical-asset specificity due to tailored machinery for a particular use.
options.B: Site specificity due to location dependence and co-location requirements.
options.C: Human-asset specificity due to nontransferable routines and tacit know-how.
options.D: No specificity because equipment is always transferable across uses.

questions.explanation: Physical-asset specificity arises when equipment is tailored for a particular customer or design and has low value in alternative uses.

questions.stem: A disciplined test for diversification is:

options.A: Are we worth more together than apart after adding coordination and governance costs.
options.B: Did the stock price rise immediately after announcing the acquisition to the market.
options.C: Did competitors complain loudly, indicating the move must be strategically sound.
options.D: Did we enter a bigger market, because growth always improves valuation.

questions.explanation: The core test is net value: parenting value-add must exceed coordination cost; market reactions are informative but not decisive.
